metadata.title: AMC Won’t Consent To Tokenized Stocks Under New SEC Rules, CEO Says: Tokens Let Brokers ‘Fool Around With Our Balance Sheet’

content.text:
-
According to Aron, the trend of tokenizing stocks accelerated by Robinhood is "terrible."
-
He warned that tokenization could make it harder for companies to control their capital structures and manage their own financial strategies.
-
The CEO said the SEC "agreed with us" when it issued rules shortly after his social media criticism of Robinhood's tokenization plans.
AMC Entertainment (AMC) CEO Adam Aron said on Thursday that the company would 'say no' to having its shares converted into digital tokens in the U.S., escalating his fight with Robinhood Markets (HOOD).
"We think this Robinhood tokenization trend is terrible," Aron told CNBC in an interview. He said new rules from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) require companies to agree before their stock can be tokenized, and that AMC plans on "saying no."
"We're going to be saying no to tokenization."
– Adam Aron, CEO, AMC Entertainment
Aron said companies should decide how their own shares are issued and traded. "We think that companies should be in charge of their own capital structures, not a brokerage company trying to fool around with our balance sheet," he said.
AMC stock edged 0.3% higher in early morning trade on Thursday. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the firm shifted to 'extremely bullish' from 'bullish' over the past day, accompanied by 'high' levels of chatter.
Why Is AMC CEO Against Stock Tokenization?
Aron stated that control over AMC's shares and debt has been central to the company's recovery. "Tokenization makes it more difficult for companies to control their own destinies, which we think is a secret to our success over the past five years," he said.
The comments follow a series of social media posts in which Aron criticized Robinhood's tokenization plans. He said the SEC "agreed with us" when it issued its rules shortly after his posts.
Aron pointed to AMC's debt reduction as evidence of the progress the company has made. In 2022, two years after the COVID-19 pandemic forced theaters to close, AMC's debt stood at 114 times its annual adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA).
He noted that, since then, AMC has paid down $2 billion of debt and refinanced another $4 billion, extending repayment dates by five to seven years. Aron expects the debt-to-adjusted EBITDA ratio to decline to between 4 and 4.5 times this year.
"That's like a normal balance sheet," he said. "It's not quite investment grade, need to say, but it's normal." He called it "a miraculous performance." AMC was recently upgraded by credit rating agencies, he added.
